summary: Sets out conventions for representing names in a friendly way and shows how the OSI Directory can then offer user-friendly naming. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 3494.

plainLanguage.summary: Writing names the way people say them instead of in strict computer form.

questions: how to write names in the osi directory
subtitle: How to represent directory names in a way people can actually read and use.

tldr.problem: The OSI Directory uses formal distinguished names that are hard for people to read or type. Systems need a way to let users refer to directory entries in natural, informal language.
tldr.mechanism: The specification defines a user-friendly name (UFN) notation that omits attribute types, allows abbreviations and approximate matches, and provides an algorithm for resolving human-readable names back to formal distinguished names through directory lookups.
tldr.outcome: Users can type or communicate directory names like "Steve Kille, Computer Science, University College London, GB" instead of formal notation, while still resolving reliably to the correct directory entry.

today: This RFC is Historic. RFC 3494 supersedes it and refines the user-friendly naming specification.

sections.title: Why Directory Names Need a User-Friendly Format
sections.content:
The OSI Directory stores information about people and organizations using Distinguished Names (DNs), which are formal hierarchical identifiers. These names are precise but unwieldy. A typical DN might be written as CN=Steve Kille, O=ISODE Consortium, C=GB. The RFC notes that directory users need a way to refer to entries in human-to-human communication—on business cards, in email, or when entering a name into a system—that does not require expertise in directory notation.

The challenge is to allow people to type or communicate directory names in a way that feels natural and informal, while still being unambiguous enough for a system to resolve them correctly. The notation defined in this RFC enables users to omit type prefixes, abbreviate paths, use approximate matches, and still have the system find the right entry.
sections.plainLanguage: Computer formats for names are hard to read. This spec lets people write names the easy way, like you would write them on a postcard, and the computer can still figure out who they mean.

sections.title: The User-Friendly Name Notation
sections.content:
A user-friendly name (UFN) omits the attribute type labels that are always present in a distinguished name. Instead of CN=Steve Kille, OU=Computer Science, O=University College London, C=GB, a user can write Steve Kille, Computer Science, University College London, GB. The system assumes that the first element is a Common Name, the last is a Country, and intermediate elements follow a standard organizational hierarchy.

The notation also allows for variations. Users can omit organizational units if they are unambiguous within context. They can use friendly names for countries (for example, "GB" or "UK" instead of a formal code). They can abbreviate components ("UCL" for "University College London") or use approximate values ("Steve" for "S. Kille") and let the directory search find the intended match. These flexibilities make the notation friendly while still enabling the system to resolve the name reliably.
sections.plainLanguage: You write the name without the computer labels, just the words in order, and the system knows from the pattern what each part means. You can also use short versions or nicknames and it will search to find what you meant.

sections.title: Resolving Names Through the Directory
sections.content:
When a user supplies a purported name—the informal version—the system must resolve it to a formal distinguished name using directory lookups. The RFC defines a matching algorithm that works in stages. It starts with a local environment, which is a ordered list of contexts (such as "Physics Department, University College London, GB" or "GB" alone) that the user's local system should search first. This context makes abbreviations possible: if the user types just "Steve Kille", the system tries to find them within the local context before broadening the search.

The algorithm recognizes three levels of match: exact matches (when a name component matches a directory value exactly), good matches (when a component is unambiguous and matches an attribute), and poor matches (substring or approximate matches). The system automatically follows exact matches, follows all good matches if no exact matches exist, and prompts the user only when it encounters ambiguous or poor matches. If the user rejects all offered matches at one environment level, the system proceeds to the next level and tries again, gradually widening the search until a match is found.
sections.plainLanguage: The system has a list of places to search (like your department, then your university, then your country). It tries each one in order. If you type a name, it looks for exact matches first, and only asks you to choose if there are several possibilities.

sections.title: Examples of the System at Work
sections.content:
The RFC provides real examples. If a user types "Joe Bloggs" in a department context, the system searches the local physics department, and returns "Joseph Z. Bloggs" without prompting. If the user types "Computer Science", the initial department search fails (because that is an organizational unit, not a person), so the system automatically tries the next environment level, finds the organizational unit, and returns it without prompting. When a user types a name with two components, such as "Andrew Findlay, Brunel", the system first resolves "Brunel" to "Brunel University, GB", then searches for "Andrew Findlay" within that organization and may return multiple matches, prompting the user to choose.

The RFC notes that experience implementing this approach at the University College London was favorable. Users found the system effective at locating known individuals with minimal effort. However, some deficiencies were noted: when an organization has multiple levels of organizational units, users who guess an intermediate level that is not directly below the organization may get poor results.
sections.plainLanguage: Examples show that if you type "Joe Bloggs" in your department, it finds him immediately. If you type "Andrew Findlay, Brunel", it first finds Brunel University, then looks for Andrew there and shows you the matches.

sections.title: Status and Relationship to Other Work
sections.content: RFC 3494 obsoletes this RFC and updates the user-friendly naming approach. The concept that user-friendly names should be possible in directory systems has remained influential, but the formal standard has evolved. The RFC's relationship to contemporary work is worth noting: it cites X.500, the formal OSI Directory standard, and credits earlier work by others on descriptive names and alternative naming approaches. The intention was always to standardize presentation conventions so that different systems could interoperate using the same informal notation.
sections.plainLanguage: This document is historic and was replaced by a newer version that refined the approach. The basic idea—letting people write names the easy way—is still used in directory systems today.
